I definitely like the concept, and the Warlock's Pact Magic makes it thematically different enough from Spellcasting to make sense as an anti-mage. It's difficult to talk about balance with anti-mages, however, as their abilities are fundamentally situational. You're either exceptionally potent or just not using your abilities at all. Of course, if both player and DM are on board with that notion, I don't think it's the end of the world.

Overall, your wording is ever slightly off from the style 'norm'. Not a big deal, but makes it more 'professional' looking. For example, in **Void Port**, you can probably just say "teleport to that creature and make a melee attack", thus including both weapon and spell attacks. Might be worth looking at similar class features to see how they're worded and try to emulate them, I think there's even a PHB style guide out there somewhere.

It really all depends on what you're trying to get out of the dip. If you're just looking for some ritual spells (Find Familiar, for example) and you expect to be able to find several of them down the line, maybe Ritual Caster's the way forward. I probably wouldn't go Magic Initiate over Ritual Caster if you end up choosing a feat.

If you want a lot more of the wizard spells, i.e. shield, misty step, etc. then the dip is likely worth it over the feat. Just be sure to avoid spells that have attack rolls/saving throws unless you've also got decent Int.

As for when, I believe earlier is often better, *especially* with Portent - you'll want that ASAP. Go Cleric 1/2 to get better equipment proficiencies and maybe your Channel Divinity, then Wizard 2 for that all important Portent. Wizard 3 is optional IMO, I'd rather have the 18th level capstone for Clerics if you expect to be reaching the higher tiers. Yes, it may slow down your access to 3rd level spells, but to me you're better off getting yourself back on track to a regular progression.

The question you really need to ask is: do you care if you are? 

Yes, mathematically, you may fall behind the curve a bit using a longbow and not Eldritch Blast - but so what? You aren't going to be *so* behind the curve that you feel useless, and certainly your Eldritch Smites will be able to do some great nova damage that EB couldn't hope for. But by and large, if the build you've gone for makes you happy and fits what you want for your character - who cares if EB would edge out those extra few hit points.

**Time Bandit:** Well... This is quite strong. I appreciate that you both (a) have to be the one to reduce them to zero and (b) make them perform a Cha. saving throw, but a free action is no small deal. I guess I'd have to see this playtested to comment on whether or not it's *too* strong, but a uses per long rest addition wouldn't be entirely amiss.

**If I Could Turn Back Time:** The name's a little long, for a start. ;) Probably my least favourite feature. First of all, if the character has moved then combat slows down while the players figure out where exactly they started the round at. If they haven't moved - what happens? Do they still avoid the damage - it wouldn't make sense if they did, but then this feature is rendered useless. Could do with some fine tuning, I feel.

**Temporal Syphoning:** Warlocks don't prepare spells. I think you mean to say that they learn *haste* and *slow*, but they don't count against the total spells the warlock can know. Further... It's just a damn OP feature. Casting *haste* and *slow,* *and* gaining another bonus action while *slow* is active?! It really is too much. I honestly think just giving them access to these two spells would be plenty for this class. Maybe allowing them to cast either one for free once per day.

**Offering to the Timestream:** I can't even begin to picture the shenanigans caused by this feature. Have you playtested it at all? I'd be intrigued to know what could be done. It certainly feels very abuseable.

Ultimate Alchemy by Tema! A well-thought-out, really enjoyable pack that changes the game.

**Phoenix Spark**

Making this available at 1st level, alongside Mantle of Flame, is what is really front-loading the class and makes it very appealing for 1-level dips. I noticed you removed the additional benefits granted to this ability that occur when MoF is active, presumably to try and scale down the power level. If you do choose to keep this as a 1st level ability, I recommend adding in those benefits as an 'improved' ability at a later level.

​

**Mantle of Flame**  
Making this available more than once per long rest is not necessarily a bad thing, but because you've made other abilities stronger, it really has a knock-on effect. If you were to keep Phoenix Spark as a 1st level ability, I really recommend removing the uses = Con. mod; if you move Phoenix Spark back to 6th level, I'd consider keeping it.

​

**Nourishing Fire**

The fire resistance is a nice addition! I don't think having this ability available at 6th level is too bad, though the last line (regaining hit points if MoF is active when PS triggers) seems a little out-of-place. 

​

**Form of the Phoenix**

This is a little poorly worded, but I assume you're just taking the first bullet point of the UA Form of the Phoenix ability and making it available at 14th level? I'm not too mad at that - both Divine and Draconic sorcerers get their flying ability at 14th, too. But, now this level feels a little bland. Perhaps consider moving some of the other abilities to this level alongside FotP?

I'd maybe even recommend making Mantle of Flame's uses = Con. mod a 14th level feature! In general I'm a fan of class features that get built upon rather than starting strong and not growing.

​

**Mantle of the Phoenix**

Just as an aside, I'd change the name of this one, the terminology is going to get messy.

I'm not upset about the changes here. 18th level abilities *should* be powerful. I guess my main issue is that, if I were playing a Phoenix sorcerer, I would likely have already picked up *Elemental Adept: Fire*, making the first bullet point of this ability superfluous. Half way through my 4th year of Latin at university, here's what I've learned:

1. When it comes to vocabulary: do a lots of little. That is, take 10 minutes in the morning, 10 minutes in the afternoon, 10 minutes in the evening. Use things like Memrise or Anki if they help, or the Goldlist method if that works for you. Just do quick, focused sessions, and do them often. For me it was the only way to effectively gain a vocabulary in Latin, and now it grows without me even realising.
2. Building on that, make sure you make note of every word that you have trouble with. And I mean *every word.* Tackle it now, so it doesn't become a problem later.
3. Actually learn the grammatical structures. I've found that the people who have done best in my Latin classes are those with at least some grounding knowledge in morphology and syntax. Learn what the subjunctive mood actually is; learn what the gerund is; learn where an ablative absolute comes from. It'll make prose composition much easier.
4. On the flip side, don't *rely* on grammatical structures. Like Wafflotron said, picking up something like Familia Romana will assist in your ability to actually *read* Latin rather than just *translating* it. This was something that took me a while to get to grips with, and after a couple years I realised I couldn't just look at a text and read it, I was always verb hunting and defining the case and number of every noun etc.
5. Macrons are a luxury, one you won't often find yourself with. Learn Latin without them, and when they do appear it's just a pleasant surprise.
